description: Become confident with the computer programs every office and business uses. Over 2 months you learn computer basics, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint, plus the internet, email and Google tools. Live classes, recorded lessons and practice on real projects. Earn a Techive certificate after a quiz and a final project.
project_brief:
Prepare a small business pack for a real or imaginary business. It has three files:

1. Word: a one-page business letter or a CV with a heading style, a table and page numbers.
2. Excel: a monthly budget or sales sheet with at least 8 rows, formulas (SUM, AVERAGE and one IF), a total row and one chart.
3. PowerPoint: a 6-slide presentation introducing the business (title, about, services, prices, why choose us, contact), using a consistent design and no more than a few words per bullet.

Put the three files in one Google Drive or OneDrive folder, set it to "anyone with the link can view", and submit the link. In the notes, say which feature you are proudest of.

lessons.title: Parts of a computer and how to use Windows
lessons.body:
A computer has hardware (the parts you can touch) and software (the programs).

- Input: keyboard, mouse, microphone.
- Processing: the CPU is the brain; RAM is short-term working memory.
- Storage: hard disk or SSD keeps your files when the computer is off.
- Output: screen, printer, speakers.

The operating system (Windows) manages everything. Learn these parts of Windows: the Desktop, the Taskbar, the Start menu, windows (minimise, maximise, close) and Settings.

Shut down properly through the Start menu instead of holding the power button, so that files are not damaged.

Practice: open three programs, switch between them with Alt+Tab, and close them all.

lessons.title: Files, folders and typing skills
lessons.body:
Files hold your work; folders organise files. Use File Explorer to create folders such as Documents > Course Work.

Key actions:
- Copy: Ctrl+C. Cut: Ctrl+X. Paste: Ctrl+V.
- Undo: Ctrl+Z. Save: Ctrl+S. Select all: Ctrl+A.
- Rename: select the file and press F2.
- Delete sends a file to the Recycle Bin, where you can restore it.

Give files clear names (CV_Amina_2026.docx, not New Document 7). Keep a backup of important files on a flash disk or cloud storage.

Typing: sit upright, keep your wrists relaxed, and use all fingers. Accuracy first, speed later. Practise 15 minutes daily with a free typing tutor.

Practice: create a folder structure for this course, and save a test file in it.

lessons.title: Getting started with Word
lessons.body:
Word is for letters, reports, CVs and assignments. Parts of the screen: the Ribbon (tabs such as Home, Insert, Layout), the ruler, the document area and the status bar.

Basics:
- Type your text first, format after.
- Select text, then use Home tab tools: Bold (Ctrl+B), Italic (Ctrl+I), Underline (Ctrl+U), font, size and colour.
- Align text: left (Ctrl+L), centre (Ctrl+E), right (Ctrl+R), justify (Ctrl+J).
- Save early (Ctrl+S) and often. Use Save As to choose the name and place.

Turn on spell check and fix words underlined in red. Read your document once more before printing.

Practice: type a short letter to a friend and format the heading, the body and the closing.

lessons.title: Paragraphs, lists and styles
lessons.body:
Make your document look professional with consistent formatting.

- Line spacing and paragraph spacing: Home > Paragraph group. 1.15 or 1.5 is easy to read.
- Bullets and numbering for lists.
- Indents and tabs for neat alignment.
- Styles: apply Heading 1, Heading 2 and Normal from the Styles gallery instead of changing each heading by hand. When you change a style, every heading using it changes at once, and a table of contents can be built from headings.

Use Format Painter (the paintbrush on the Home tab) to copy formatting from one place to another.

Practice: write a one-page report with a title, two Heading 2 sections and a bulleted list.

modules.title: Week 3: Word for work and school

lessons.title: Tables, pictures and page layout
lessons.body:
Tables arrange information in rows and columns: Insert > Table. Use Table Design to change colours and borders, and Layout to add rows, merge cells and align text.

Pictures: Insert > Pictures, then drag the corner handles to resize. Use Wrap Text to place a picture beside text.

Page layout:
- Margins, orientation (portrait or landscape) and size (A4) under the Layout tab.
- Page numbers: Insert > Page Number.
- Headers and footers for names and titles.
- Page breaks (Ctrl+Enter) to start a new page.

Before printing, use File > Print to see a preview.

Practice: create a price list table with 5 rows, add page numbers and a footer with your name.

lessons.title: Professional documents: CV, letters and mail merge
lessons.body:
A good CV is short (1-2 pages), clear and honest. Typical sections: name and contact, profile, education, experience or projects, skills, referees. Use one readable font (such as Calibri or Arial) at 11 or 12 pt, consistent headings and plenty of white space.

Formal letter order: your address, date, receiver's address, greeting (Dear Sir/Madam), subject line, body, closing (Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely) and signature.

Mail merge sends the same letter to many people with their own names: Mailings > Start Mail Merge, select recipients from an Excel list, insert merge fields like <<Name>>, then finish and merge.

Practice: write your CV in Word and save it as a PDF (File > Save As > PDF).

lessons.title: Getting to know Excel
lessons.body:
Excel is a spreadsheet program for numbers, lists, budgets and records. A file is a workbook with sheets. Each sheet has columns (A, B, C...), rows (1, 2, 3...) and cells named by column and row, for example B3.

Basics:
- Click a cell and type. Press Enter to move down, Tab to move right.
- Select a range by dragging, for example A1:A10.
- Widen a column by double-clicking the line between column letters.
- Use Bold, fill colour and borders on the Home tab to make headings clear.
- Insert or delete rows and columns by right-clicking the number or letter.

Keep one table per sheet, with headings in the first row and no blank rows inside the data.

Practice: build a list of 8 items with names, quantities and prices.

lessons.title: Your first formulas
lessons.body:
A formula always starts with =. Excel calculates it and updates when numbers change.

=B2*C2       multiply quantity by price
=SUM(D2:D9)  add a range
=AVERAGE(B2:B9)
=MAX(B2:B9)   =MIN(B2:B9)
=COUNT(B2:B9)

Operators: + - * / and ^ (power). Excel follows brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

Autofill: after writing a formula, drag the small square in the corner of the cell down to copy it to the rows below. Excel adjusts the cell names automatically (relative references).

If you see ####, widen the column. If you see #DIV/0!, you divided by zero.

Practice: add a Total column that multiplies quantity by price, then a SUM at the bottom.

lessons.title: Cell references and the IF function
lessons.body:
A relative reference such as B2 changes when copied. An absolute reference such as $B$2 stays fixed (press F4 to add the dollar signs). Use it when every row must use the same cell, for example a VAT rate in $F$1: =D2*$F$1.

The IF function makes decisions:

=IF(B2>=50,"Pass","Fail")

It means: if B2 is at least 50 then show Pass, otherwise show Fail. You can nest IFs for several grades, but keep them simple.

Other helpful functions: ROUND(number, digits), TODAY(), COUNTIF(range, criteria) to count items that meet a rule, and SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) to add only matching rows.

Practice: create a marks sheet with a Pass/Fail column using IF, and count the passes with COUNTIF.

lessons.title: Lookups, sorting and filtering
lessons.body:
Sorting puts data in order (Data > Sort). Filtering shows only the rows you want (Data > Filter, then the drop-down arrows). Both work best on a clean table with a header row.

VLOOKUP finds a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from another column:

=VLOOKUP(A2, $F$2:$G$20, 2, FALSE)

This looks for A2 in the first column of F2:G20 and returns the value in column 2. FALSE means exact match. Newer versions of Excel also have XLOOKUP, which does the same job more flexibly.

Data validation (Data > Data Validation) can restrict a cell to a drop-down list, which prevents typing mistakes.

Practice: build a small product price list, then use VLOOKUP to fetch a price by product name.

modules.title: Week 6: Excel charts and real-life sheets

lessons.title: Charts that tell a story
lessons.body:
Charts turn numbers into pictures. Select your data including the headings, then Insert > Recommended Charts.

- Column or bar chart: compare categories (sales per month).
- Line chart: show change over time.
- Pie chart: show parts of a whole, for a small number of slices.

Improve your chart: add a clear title, label the axes, remove clutter and use readable colours. One chart should make one point.

Pivot tables (Insert > PivotTable) summarise large lists quickly, for example total sales per product. Drag fields into Rows and Values. They are worth learning once you are comfortable with basic tables.

Practice: make a column chart of monthly sales and give it a title and axis labels.

lessons.title: Build a monthly budget and sales sheet
lessons.body:
Apply everything you learned in one practical sheet.

Budget layout:
- Column A: Item (Rent, Transport, Airtime, Food, Savings).
- Column B: Planned amount. Column C: Actual amount. Column D: Difference =B2-C2.
- Total row with =SUM().
- A status column: =IF(D2<0,"Over budget","OK").

Format the money with a thousands separator (Home > Number group). Freeze the top row (View > Freeze Panes) so headings stay visible. Use conditional formatting (Home > Conditional Formatting) to colour overspent rows red.

Protect your work: save often, keep a backup copy, and double-check formulas by testing with easy numbers.

Practice: build your own budget for a month and add a chart of planned versus actual.

lessons.title: Creating clear presentations
lessons.body:
PowerPoint helps you present ideas with slides. Start with the story, not the design: what is the one message of each slide?

Basics:
- New Slide chooses a layout (Title, Title and Content, Two Content).
- Use Design > Themes for a consistent look. Do not change fonts and colours on every slide.
- Slide Master (View > Slide Master) changes all slides at once.
- Present with F5 (from the start) or Shift+F5 (from this slide).

Good design rules: one idea per slide, large text (24 pt or more), 3 to 5 short bullets, high contrast between text and background, one or two fonts, and pictures that add meaning.

Practice: create a 5-slide presentation about yourself or your business.

lessons.title: Pictures, transitions and presenting with confidence
lessons.body:
Pictures, icons, charts and simple shapes keep the audience interested. Insert > Pictures, Icons or Chart (you can paste an Excel chart). Align objects with the Align tool so slides look neat.

Transitions (the effect between slides) and animations (effects inside slides) should be simple. Too many effects distract.

Presenting tips:
- Practise aloud at least twice. Time yourself.
- Do not read from the slide. Slides support you; you tell the story.
- Face the audience, speak slowly and pause.
- Prepare a backup copy on a flash disk and as a PDF (File > Export).
- Check the projector and sound before you start.

Practice: present your 5 slides to a friend or family member and ask for one improvement.

modules.title: Week 8: Internet, email, cloud tools and final project

lessons.title: Internet, email, cloud storage and staying safe
lessons.body:
Use a browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) to search and to open websites. Better searching: use specific words, put exact phrases in quotes, and check who published the page.

Email: a good message has a clear subject, a greeting, a short body and a polite closing. Use Cc for people who should only be informed. Attach files with the paperclip and check the attachment is there before sending.

Cloud tools such as Google Drive, Google Docs, Google Sheets, Google Meet or OneDrive let you store files online, share a link and work together in real time. Check the sharing setting before sending a link (view only, comment or edit).

Staying safe:
- Use long, different passwords and turn on two-step verification.
- Do not click links or open attachments from people you do not know.
- Never share a password or an M-Pesa PIN with anyone.

Practice: upload a file to cloud storage and share it as view-only with a friend.

lessons.title: Final project and what comes next
lessons.body:
Bring everything together in your final project. Follow the project brief on this page: a Word letter or CV, an Excel budget or sales sheet with formulas and a chart, and a 6-slide PowerPoint, saved in one shared folder.

Before submitting, check:
- Files have clear names.
- Spelling is checked.
- Formulas give correct totals (test with easy numbers).
- The folder link is set to "anyone with the link can view".

When the tutor approves your project and you pass the quiz, you can get your Techive certificate.

What next? These skills help in office jobs, in business record keeping and in college. You can continue with the free Website Development with AI course or the free Python Programming course. Also share your referral link: when a friend you referred pays for this course, you earn a reward.
